content: 1. Vandetanib inhibits the uptake of substrates of organic cation transporter type 2 (OCT2). This interaction necessitates close monitoring when co-administered with other drugs. 2. Cimetidine increases the levels or effects of vardenafil by interfering with hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 3. Cimetidine increases varenicline levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is considered minor, but its clinical significance is unknown. 4. Cimetidine increases the levels or effects of verapamil through competition for renal tubular clearance of basic (cationic) drugs. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be considered. 5. Cimetidine also increases verapamil levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 6. Cimetidine increases the levels of vilazodone by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 7. If intolerable adverse effects occur when cimetidine is co-administered with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, the daily dose should be reduced to 20 mg. 8. Cimetidine increases vinblastine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Cimetidine increases vincristine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Cimetidine increases vincristine liposomal levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 11. Cimetidine increases vinorelbine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 12. Cimetidine decreases vismodegib levels or effects through mechanisms not fully understood. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Drugs that increase gastric pH can alter vismodegib solubility, reducing its bioavailability. The effect on efficacy is unknown. 14. Voriconazole increases cimetidine levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C19 metabolism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 15. Cimetidine increases voriconazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 16. Cimetidine increases the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be used. 17. Cimetidine increases zaleplon levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Cimetidine increases ziprasidone levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Cimetidine increases zolmitriptan levels through an unknown mechanism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. 20. Cimetidine increases zolpidem levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 21. Cimetidine increases zonisamide levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 22. Common side effects of cimetidine include confusion (especially in the elderly), impotence, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and hypersensitivity reactions. It may also cause feminization and sexual dysfunction in males due to antiandrogenic effects. 23. Patients should consult their doctor or pharmacist before taking cimetidine with other prescription drugs. 24. Cimetidine is classified as Pregnancy Category B, meaning it is generally considered safe during pregnancy based on controlled studies showing no evidence of fetal risk. However, it enters breast milk and is not recommended during lactation. 25. Cimetidine is an H2-receptor antagonist that blocks H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, leading to reduced gastric acid secretion. 26. The bioavailability of cimetidine when taken orally is 60-70%, with minimal first-pass metabolism. It is 15-20% protein-bound and metabolized in the liver, producing inactive metabolites such as cimetidine sulfoxide and 5-hydroxymethyl derivatives. 27. Cimetidine inhibits hepatic microsomal enzymes, including CYP1A2, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4, which can affect the metabolism of other drugs. 28. Cimetidine can be administered intramuscularly without dilution, via slow direct intravenous injection over 5 minutes or more after dilution to 20 mL with a compatible diluent (e.g., normal saline), or as an intermittent or continuous intravenous infusion. 29. Cimetidine is compatible with various additives, including cefazolin, clindamycin, epinephrine, erythromycin, furosemide, gentamicin, lidocaine, norepinephrine, potassium chloride, vancomycin, verapamil, and vitamins B/C. 30. Cimetidine is incompatible with certain drugs, such as carbenicillin and tetracycline, and should not be mixed with these agents. 31. Cimetidine is used to treat and prevent stomach and intestinal ulcers, as well as conditions caused by excessive stomach acid, such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, erosive esophagitis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). 32. It is also used to relieve symptoms of acid indigestion, heartburn, and sour stomach, and to prevent these symptoms when triggered by specific foods or beverages. 33. Patients using cimetidine for self-treatment should carefully follow the manufacturer's instructions and consult a doctor or pharmacist if needed. 34. The dosage and duration of cimetidine treatment depend on the patient's medical condition and response to therapy. It should be taken regularly as prescribed to achieve maximum benefit. 35. Patients should not increase their dose or take cimetidine more frequently than directed. Even if symptoms improve, the medication should be continued for the prescribed duration. 36. For self-treatment of acid indigestion or heartburn, one tablet should be taken with water as needed. To prevent heartburn, one tablet should be taken with water up to 30 minutes before consuming trigger foods or beverages. 37. Patients should not exceed two tablets in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor. 38. Common side effects of cimetidine include headache, dizziness, drowsiness, and diarrhea. Serious allergic reactions are rare. 39. Before taking cimetidine, patients should inform their doctor of any allergies, especially to H2 blockers like famotidine, nizatidine, or ranitidine, as well as any other medical conditions. 40. Liquid forms of cimetidine may contain sugar or alcohol, requiring caution in patients with diabetes, liver disease, or other conditions requiring dietary restrictions. 41. Cimetidine may cause dizziness or drowsiness, which can be exacerbated by alcohol or marijuana. Patients should avoid driving or operating machinery until they can do so safely. 42. Older adults may be more sensitive to cimetidine's side effects, particularly confusion and pneumonia. 43. During pregnancy, cimetidine should only be used when clearly needed. It passes into breast milk and is not recommended during breastfeeding. 44. Cimetidine can interact with other medications, altering their effects or increasing the risk of side effects. Patients should keep a list of all medications and share it with their healthcare provider. 45. Cimetidine may slow the elimination of other drugs from the body, potentially affecting their efficacy or safety. It may also alter the absorption of certain medications by reducing stomach acid. 46. Smoking can affect the efficacy of cimetidine. Lifestyle changes, such as stress reduction, smoking cessation, limiting alcohol, and dietary modifications, may enhance the medication's effectiveness. 47. Patients should store cimetidine at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and properly discard expired or unused medication. 48. In case of overdose, patients should seek immediate medical attention or contact a poison control center.
